newsitem.title: SPAIN: ETA expulsions dampen peace talk hopes in Spain.
newsitem.headline: ETA expulsions dampen peace talk hopes in Spain.

text.p: The Dominican Republic's expulsion to Spain of former mediators for the Basque guerrilla group ETA has dampened hopes for future peace negotiations between the separatist rebels and the Madrid government.
The Dominican Republic handed over three ETA members to Spain on Saturday, two of whom represented the group in talks in Algeria in 1989 with Spain's Socialist government of the time.
Moderate Basque politicians and ETA's political arm Herri Batasuna said on Sunday the expulsions had closed an important avenue for dialogue.
"Evidently, (Prime Minister Jose Maria) Aznar's government does not want to take steps on the road to a political solution," Herri Batasuna spokesman Floren Aoiz said on Sunday.

Political analysts said with the expulsions, the government was sending ETA a clear message it was not interested in any negotiations after the group killed Basque town councillor Miguel Angel Blanco last month.

Since Blanco's killing, which provoked national outrage, the government has been pressing for increased international cooperation as part of its crackdown on ETA. It rejects any peace talks until ETA abandons violence.

On Saturday night, a Spanish Air Force plane touched down at Torrejon air base near Madrid with the three ETA members aboard. They were identified as Eugenio Etxebeste, alias Antxon, Ignacio Aracama Mendia, alias Macario, and Jose Maria Ganchegiz.
Etxebeste, 46, led ETA's delegation to the peace talks with the former government and was instrumental in securing a two-month ceasefire from ETA during the talks. Aracama was also a negotiator.
After the talks fell apart, the three were deported to the Dominican Republic. Extebeste remained a channel for messages between the government and ETA.
The violent Basque separatist movement has on many occasions since pointed to the Dominican group as the address for any future peace negotiations with the government.

"This closes the door to a possible dialogue" said Inigo Urkullu, a spokesman for the moderate Basque Nationalist Party in the regional capital of Vitoria. His party heads the government of the autonomous Basque region.

Interior Minister Jaime Mayor Oreja said on Saturday the expulsions did not signal a toughening of the government's position, adding he saw no advantage to the deportees remaining on the Caribbean island.

"Nothing was open or closed because the so-called window of Santo Domingo or what was known as the 'mediation apparatus' was in reality a farce which only served as an international loudspeaker for ETA," Mayor Oreja said.
Some nevertheless saw a ray of hope in the expulsions.

"Another possibility is they brought the interlocutors closer because this avenue of mediation should be maintained here in the Spanish state," said Rafael Arena, spokesman for the Eusko Alkartasuna, a nationalist party in the Basque region.
ETA (Basque Homeland and Freedom) has been fighting for 29 years for an independent state. The group has killed more than 800 people.

State radio said the three would probably be arraigned on Tuesday. Aracama, 46, faces the most serious charges. He is suspected of participating in a kidnapping and in the assassinations of eight people including police, paramilitary Civil Guardsmen and a central bank official.
